newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls vs yen as Japanese official's remarks little help.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls vs yen as Japanese official's remarks little help.

text.p: The dollar fell to a one-month low against the yen Monday as comments from a key Japanese official failed to reverse market perception that Japan has abandoned its weak-yen, strong-dollar policy, currency dealers said.
As a result, the weakened dollar fell against the German mark below a technically critical support level to hit a bottom of 1.4910 marks, its lowest level since 1.4880 marks on Sept. 9.
"We took out that support against the mark and the outlook now doesn't look too good anywhere for the dollar," said Tom Hoge, vice president of corporate trading at the Bank of New York.

Director General of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau Eisuke Sakakibara, whose comments on Thursday sparked the biggest plunge in the dollar against the yen in nearly 1-1/2 years, spoke again on Monday.
However, his statement only fleetingly helped the dollar against the yen, traders said.

Sakakibara said Monday that Japan's foreign exchange policy was unchanged. This failed to reverse market conclusions, drawn from his statements last week, that Japan will no longer back the long-standing depreciation of the yen against the dollar and that economic fundmentals have begun to shift in favour of the yen.
The dollar hit a post World War Two low of 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995, but has climbed sharply since then.
"We are seeing repercussions from Sakakibara's non-denial of his statements the other night," said Russ Lascala, head of the spot currency trading desk at Citibank.

"Everyone was waiting for a flat out denial and it never happened. We're concluding that this is exactly what the Japanese wanted to happen -- dollar/yen consolidation back to the 105 to 112 area," he added.
The dollar dropped to 111.00 yen in late trading from 111.73 yen at Friday's close and hit a one-month intraday low of 110.90 yen.
Against the mark, the dollar pierced strong support at 1.5000 marks to fall to 1.4935 marks in late trade, down from Friday's close of 1.5047 marks.
The break below 1.50 triggered some technical selling and dealers said it could portend additional losses in the future.
"I think it is just a matter of time until we have a follow through of consolidation, maybe to 1.4850 (marks)," Lascala said.

A trader at a German bank said a sizable amount of British sterling was sold for marks. Given that trade volume was unusually light due to the U.S. Veteran's Day holiday, the buying helped bolster the mark.
"It's possible an order to sell sterling/mark in a thin market had a larger-than-usual impact," Hoge said.

Comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer following a Group of 10 central bank governors meeting that the currency market is relatively quiet and that Italy's inflation outlook had improved had little market impact, dealers said.
Trading in the United States wound down early because of the holiday and some bourses in Europe were closed.

The dollar continued to recover from the 33-month low set Friday versus the Canadian currency at Canadian $1.3263. The U.S. currency was quoted late Monday at Canadian $1.3338, up from Canadian $1.3315 in late North American trading on Friday.
Against the Swiss franc, the dollar fell another centime to end at 1.2545, down from 1.2645 late Friday. Traders said the move was amplified by the thin market.
